title: TDDR Rising Narratives — Wednesday evening, Nov 18
summary: A snapshot of opposition narratives from the Right and the Far Left as of 5:45 PM ET Wednesday, Nov 18, 2026. Built for TDDR (Too Dumb Didn't Read). House Democrats nominated Hakeem Jeffries for speaker this morning, 251-11, by secret ballot, and the Far Left's AIPAC attack hit its peak anyway: the Jeffries/AIPAC petition query reached 6,296 posts in 24 hours (7.67× its prior average), 2,787 of them since 7 AM. Seven of the 11 no votes, all incoming progressives, said talks with Jeffries are ongoing. New on the left: Jeffries's refusal at The Atlantic Summit to back defunding the Iran war, plus openness to a continuing resolution past Dec. 11, drew 'already caving' attacks (2,286 posts, 1.76×). New on the Right, and the top score tonight: Sen. Ron Johnson called Social Security 'a Ponzi scheme' on Fox Business and said 'you just shut it down,' then called it 'imprecise' at his own hearing. That query went from 16 posts in Tuesday's daytime hours to 4,172 today, and 'Social Security,' 'Ponzi' and 'Ron Johnson' were all on the U.S. trends list. Most of the volume is Democrats attacking him; PolitiFact has rated the same comparison False when others made it. Rep. Ayanna Pressley's 'Majority Priorities' list, with reparations (H.R. 40) first, pushed the reparations query to 2,528 posts as the Right frames it as the new majority's real agenda; H.R. 40 is a study commission and no vote is scheduled. Four cards faded and were dropped: the Texas gun bills, Slotkin 'color revolution,' Buttigieg student debt, and the Pressley speakership challenge, which ended with the vote. Every count, quote, and fact-check comes from sources and X queries pulled this evening or carried over from this morning and labeled. Nothing here is invented.

Video games (GTA 6, GTA VI, Rockstar, Vice City), baseball and college basketball dominated. 'Social Security,' 'Ponzi' and 'Ron Johnson' match the new Social Security card, which received the trend bonus. 'Al Green' reflects an X News story on the Texas Democrat demanding Trump's impeachment over Iran war powers at a House hearing; we did not score it. 'Rutgers' was on the list, but X News tied it mainly to the Notre Dame–Rutgers basketball game, so the Bovino card did not get the bonus. 'Kilmeade' and 'Temu Obama' did not match any scored query, and an X News search for 'Temu Obama' returned no U.S. story, so we did not research them further. We requested tweet_count, but the trend objects did not include it, so trend volumes are unavailable and we did not estimate them.

oppositionNote.body: Right = narratives the Right is pushing after the Democratic midterm wave. Far Left = pressure on Democratic leadership and the incoming majority from the party's left. Tonight the Dec. 11 funding deadline is attacked from both sides: the Right says Democrats want a 'third shutdown,' while the left says Jeffries won't use it to defund the Iran war. The Social Security card is tagged Right because the 'Ponzi scheme' frame is a Right talking point, even though most of the posts matching it are Democratic backlash. The Right also reshares the Jeffries fights as a 'Democratic civil war.' The tag is the primary opposition frame.

methodology: Last updated Wednesday, Nov 18, 2026, 5:45 PM ET. This is a research snapshot for TDDR, not a live API, and it will go stale overnight. U.S. X trends were pulled at about 5:12 PM ET. This morning's snapshot (Nov 18, 7:20 AM ET) is kept in the archive and was not overwritten. Fifteen of its nineteen narratives were re-counted with the same queries so momentum compares like with like. The new 24-hour window overlaps this morning's by 14 hours (5 PM Tuesday to 7 AM Wednesday ET), so we also report each query's 7 AM–5 PM ET Wednesday count against the same hours Tuesday. Four narratives were dropped because they faded: the Texas gun bills (133 posts in the last 24 hours, 0.11× its prior daily average), Slotkin 'color revolution' (168 posts, 0.15×), Buttigieg on student debt (141 posts, 0.82×), and Pressley's speakership challenge (654 posts, 0.09×), which ended with Wednesday's vote. Two were added with new queries: Ron Johnson's Social Security 'Ponzi scheme' remarks and the left's backlash to Jeffries on Iran war funding. One candidate was counted and not carved out as a card: Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed's plan to take his oath on a Quran, which Gov. Ron DeSantis answered with a Jefferson letter (2,817 posts, 0.40×; 1,178 from 7 AM to 5 PM ET versus 2,928 the same hours Tuesday). The outage + cyberattack query reported inside the FAA card was not re-pulled this evening.

For each narrative we ran one English-language X search with x.get_posts_counts_recent at hourly granularity over a 167-hour window from 6:00 PM ET Wednesday, Nov 11 (the earliest whole-hour start the recent-count API allowed at pull time), through 5:00 PM ET Wednesday, Nov 18. The last 24 hourly buckets (5:00 PM ET Tuesday, Nov 17, through 5:00 PM ET Wednesday, Nov 18, exactly 24 hours) give the 24-hour count, and the whole window gives the 'seven-day' total. We counted named news or fact-check outlets whose coverage we opened or retrieved in this evening's searches and cite on the card. Official government pages, bill text, advocacy groups, research groups, pollsters, bill trackers, blogs, X News summaries, and X posts are cited as sources but not counted as outlets. We re-researched the Jeffries/AIPAC and reparations cards, plus the two new cards, and counted only outlets retrieved this evening on those cards, which is why some of their outlet counts changed. For the other cards, which we did not re-research this evening, the outlet count is carried over from this morning, and each of those cards says so. We noted whether each topic appeared on the U.S. trends list at about 5:12 PM ET.

Score = 50% volume index + 30% acceleration index + 20% coverage index. Volume index is 100 × log10(1 + last-24h posts) / log10(1 + the highest last-24h count in this set). Acceleration index is 100 × min(last-24h / prior daily average, 3) / 3, so a triple-or-higher average scores 100. Prior daily average is (seven-day total − last 24h) / 6. Coverage index is 70 × min(outlets, 7) / 7, plus 30 if the topic was on the U.S. X trends list this evening. The Social Security, Arizona, shutdown and 'Make America Nice Again' queries had low baselines, so their acceleration indices are maxed out or nearly so on modest volume. Read the post counts alongside the scores. Morning-to-evening score changes also reflect the lower volume ceiling (7,753 this evening versus 9,465 this morning) and how much coverage we retrieved.

Counts are query matches, not unique posts or unique users, and queries can overlap. The Jeffries/AIPAC, Jeffries Iran funding, Jeffries ATM and DSA queries share many speaker-race posts. The Social Security query also catches posts attacking Johnson, which were most of the sample. The AOC query includes the bare word 'cast,' the shutdown query needs both 'shutdown' and an Iran/Medicaid/deadline term, and the rigged-midterms query also catches posts mocking fraud claims. Replies are included, and automated @grok replies make up a visible share of several queries. Sentiment is a qualitative label from relevancy-sorted post samples and from quotes in news coverage, not a scientific poll. This evening we pulled fresh samples for the Jeffries/AIPAC, Jeffries Iran funding, reparations and Social Security queries. Other cards carry this morning's sentiment and say so. Daily bar charts use UTC days (a UTC day starts at 7:00 PM ET the previous evening). Bars marked * are partial windows. Hourly charts are labeled in ET.

disinfo.caveatBody: New this evening: 'Social Security is a Ponzi scheme' is a comparison PolitiFact has rated False when others made it, and Sen. Ron Johnson himself called his 'shut it down' line 'imprecise' hours later. 'Pressley's H.R. 40 pays reparations' is misleading: it creates a study commission, and no floor vote is scheduled. 'Jeffries backs the Iran war' is false as stated: he opposes the war and pledged a war powers vote, but rejected defunding it. Posts claiming pro-Israel members delivered Jeffries's 251-11 win are guesses, since the ballot was secret. The '1.2 million signatures' figure against Jeffries remains unverified. Carried over from this morning: there is still no evidence this week's outages were a cyberattack (Rubio: 'zero evidence'); 'Arizona Democrats are running a bill to legalize ballot harvesting' is unconfirmed; 'Democrats will defund the military to shut down the government' is misleading, since the push is about Iran-war funds; 'AOC is an actor who answered a casting call' twists a real, public recruitment; 'Jeffries took $1.5 million from AIPAC' conflates different money streams; Lead Stories found no '30,000-case' Texas voter fraud probe; and the Texas reparations bill (SB 376) does not pay reparations and is only prefiled.

narratives.title: NEW: 'Social Security is a Ponzi scheme' — Ron Johnson says 'shut it down,' then walks it back
narratives.query: ("Ron Johnson" OR "Social Security") (Ponzi OR "Ponzi scheme") lang:en
narratives.sentiment: Mostly furious backlash; a smaller Right camp cheering 'it's a scam'
narratives.sentimentNote: In a relevancy sample of posts since 7 AM ET Wednesday, most top matches quoted Johnson's 'shut it down' line to attack him and 'MAGA' ('Leave my Social Security alone,' 'Has he heard of Trump's crypto?'), with one account pasting the same reply dozens of times. The Right's version circulated through RealClearPolitics ('Young People Should Be Furious') and @LeadingReport's 'legal Ponzi scheme' post, the most-liked post we saw. X News also summarized a Johnson committee report calling the program a 'legal Ponzi scheme.' This is a read of that sample, not a poll.
narratives.summary: New this evening, and on the U.S. trends list ('Social Security,' 'Ponzi' and 'Ron Johnson' all appeared at about 5:12 PM ET). The query matched 5,249 posts in the last 24 hours, against a prior daily average of 45.2, so its acceleration is capped; 4,172 of them came from 7 AM to 5 PM ET Wednesday, versus 16 in the same hours Tuesday. The busiest hour was 12 PM Wednesday (569 posts). On Fox Business Wednesday morning, Sen. Ron Johnson (R-Wis.), the Senate Budget Committee chairman, said: 'At this point, there's really no way to fix Social Security. It's a Ponzi scheme. You can't fix it, you just shut it down and hope that you can recover some of your money' (The Hill, HuffPost, MarketWatch). He made a similar case on Newsmax, citing the SEC's definition of a Ponzi scheme (MS NOW). At his hearing, 'Social Security: The Reality,' Sen. Ron Wyden said it was the first time in decades a senior senator said he would rather shut the program down than fix it; Johnson answered that his statement was 'imprecise' and that he is 'not proposing shutting down Social Security' (The Hill). An X News summary says a Johnson committee report projects trust-fund depletion by 2032 and calls the program a 'legal Ponzi scheme.' MarketWatch cites the CBO: if the trust funds run out, benefits could fall about 26%. This is a Right narrative that mostly spread as a Democratic attack; we score it because the 'Ponzi' frame itself is moving, and because it previews the 2027 fight over the payroll tax cap.
talkingPoints: Social Security is a Ponzi scheme: today's workers pay today's retirees.
Young people will never see a dime of what they paid in.
It's not your money — Congress already spent it.
It's going broke by 2032 and nobody in Washington will say so.
Let workers invest in the market instead.
narratives.amplifiers: Right: @SenRonJohnson (Fox Business and Newsmax appearances); @LeadingReport ('legal Ponzi scheme,' 1,501 likes, 92 reposts, 44,891 views); @RCPolitics. Backlash: @atrupar's clips (quoted by MS NOW), Democratic Sens. Ruben Gallego and Tammy Baldwin per X News, @DemsReporter, and Social Security Works. X News ran two summaries.
narratives.whyItWorks: 'Ponzi scheme' is a sticky, intuitive metaphor for a pay-as-you-go system, and genuine insolvency projections give it a factual hook. It speaks to young workers' fear that they pay in and get nothing, and it moves the debate from 'how to fix' to 'whether to keep.' For Democrats, the 'shut it down' quote is a gift, which is why the backlash outran the original.
narratives.audience: Libertarian and fiscal-conservative voters, younger right-leaning men skeptical of entitlements, and Fox Business/Newsmax audiences. The backlash reaches seniors, Wisconsin voters and the broad Democratic base.
narratives.counter: Use his own walk-back: even Johnson now says he isn't proposing to shut it down. Then explain the difference: a Ponzi scheme is a fraud that hides how it works; Social Security is a public, legally mandated program that can be kept solvent by changing taxes or benefits (PolitiFact). Name the fix: lifting the payroll tax cap ($184,500 in 2026, per The Hill) closes much of the gap without cutting benefits.

factChecks.claim: Social Security is a Ponzi scheme.
factChecks.detail: PolitiFact rated Rick Perry's Ponzi comparison False in 2011 and, reviewing the same claim from Elon Musk in 2025, said that unlike a Ponzi scheme Social Security is transparent, has oversight, promises no unrealistic returns, and can be made solvent through changes to taxes or benefits. It also noted the superficial similarity: current workers' taxes pay current retirees. PolitiFact has not rated Johnson's Nov. 18 remark.

factChecks.rating: He said it, then retracted it
factChecks.detail: On Fox Business he said 'you just shut it down.' Hours later, at his own hearing, he called that 'imprecise' and said he is 'not proposing shutting down Social Security' (The Hill). He has long proposed making Social Security discretionary spending, subject to annual appropriations (HuffPost). This is TDDR's read of that reporting, not a rating from a fact-check outlet.

Posts recirculated his pro-Israel PAC totals and old AIPAC speeches, and an X News summary of the vote repeated the '1.2 million signatures' petition figure, which we still could not verify. X News also clustered a CODEPINK video of activists pressing Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez on why no progressive challenged Jeffries, and a fight over Mehdi Hasan calling him one of the Hill's worst speakers. House Democrats vote behind closed doors this morning. Axios reports offices are still being flooded with calls but members expect Jeffries to win easily: nobody is challenging him, Rep. Jamie Raskin has ruled it out, Pressley has privately told colleagues she is not running, and Rep.-elect Jake Johnson (D-Minn.), who had been undecided, now says he will vote for Jeffries after being 'assured' votes on ending tariffs and the Iran war. He calls Jerusalem New York's 'sixth borough' and wants to be your speaker.
The 11 'no' votes are the only Democrats who listened to voters.

Point to concrete wins (AOC leading the healthcare working group, a promised early war-powers vote) and separate verified money figures from inflated ones: OpenSecrets data show far less from AIPAC itself than the viral totals.
